I am a lawyer. Admittedly I'm a commercial litigator but the principles of cross examination and discrediting witnesses are the same whether they're giving evidence of the formation of a contract or giving evidence of sexual consent.

There are nuanced aspects of evidence law which prevent lawyers from running a straight up "she was a slut" kind of cross examination. The prosecutor will object on relevance 100 times out of 100 and the objection will ordinarily be upheld. The same as to what she was wearing.

Lay people don't really understand the relevance requirement as a rule of evidence. If you want to ask questions they have to be relevant to the issues in the trial. In most circumstances, the issues in a rape case are whether sexual penetration ever occurred or as to the existence of consent. A history of promiscuity, the complainant's clothing at the time, etc. are very rarely relevant to those questions.

Yes, you can make the victim look like a slut who was begging for it but only in the context of the event itself. And obviously you would because the only real rebuttal to "He had sex with me against my will" is "no, she wanted me to fuck her". In most contexts the latter is implicitly an accusation that she's a bit loose with her affections.

EDIT: I should add that calling a potential rape victim a slut or making her cry in court doesn't normally play well to a jury. For the same reason we ditch our french-cuffed shirts and armani suits on court days the "bulldog lawyer" cross examination you might see on TV doesn't really exist in real life. You have to appear human and have a jury like you. A good cross examination is more of a pickpocketing than a mugging, it's about what you leave unsaid. When you finish with the witness he or she should really have no idea what it is you asked them that is damaging to their case. You get just enough out of them so that you can ram the point home in closing submissions but you rarely break them on the stand. It's why real trials are not fun to watch.
